```{python}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

import numpy as np
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import json, pathlib
from IPython.display import HTML, display

rng = np.random.default_rng(20260824)

C = {
    "blue":   "#2c6e9b",
    "orange": "#d1743a",
    "green":  "#4f8f63",
    "red":    "#b5483d",
    "grey":   "#9aa3ab",
    "dark":   "#2c4a63",
}

mu_hw = np.array([170.0, 75.0])
sd_hw = np.array([10.0, 15.0])
S_hw  = np.outer(sd_hw, sd_hw) * np.array([[1.0, 0.7], [0.7, 1.0]])
```

You randomise a few hundred people into two arms, then look at the baseline
table. The treatment group is a year older, and — because age and blood pressure
travel together — slightly more hypertensive. Nothing has gone wrong. This is
what randomisation does, and it will happen for roughly one covariate in twenty
however many you check. But you now get to spend the rest of the study
explaining it, and the imbalance sits in your standard errors whether you
explain it or not.

Rerandomization takes the obvious way out: draw a split, measure how unbalanced
it is, and if it is bad, throw it away and draw another. The result is still a
genuinely random assignment, drawn from a smaller pool of good ones. It all
happens before a single unit is treated, and it costs nothing but CPU time.

This article answers the two questions a practitioner actually has.

## What it does

Imbalance is scored with the Mahalanobis distance from
[the previous article](../mahalanobis-distance/), which collapses a whole
covariate table into one number without double-counting covariates that say the
same thing. With $N$ units, $k$ covariates and two equal arms:

::: {.keybox}
$$
M \;=\; \frac{N}{4}\,
        (\bar X_T - \bar X_C)^{\!\top}\, S^{-1} (\bar X_T - \bar X_C)
$$

$S$ is the covariate covariance matrix of all $N$ units, and
$\bar X_T, \bar X_C$ are the two arms' covariate means. Accept the split if $M$
is small enough, otherwise draw again.
:::

Two things about that formula. $S$ describes the pool of units, not the split,
so **compute it once, outside the loop** — along with whatever factorisation you
use to apply $S^{-1}$. And the $N/4$ is what puts $M$ on a $\chi^2_k$ scale,
which is what makes thresholds interpretable.

## Does it buy you enough to bother?

Short answer: **it depends almost entirely on whether your covariates predict
the outcome, and barely at all on how hard you rerandomize.**

The precision you gain shows up as a smaller standard error on the treatment
effect, shrunk by a factor of $\sqrt{1 - (1 - v_a)R^2}$. Only two things enter:
$R^2$, the share of outcome variance your balanced covariates explain, and
$v_a$, the fraction of imbalance the rerandomization leaves behind — which is
essentially zero unless you are balancing a lot of covariates.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-gain
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'How much smaller your standard error gets, for a 1-in-10,000 acceptance rate. Columns are the share of outcome variance explained by the covariates you balanced. Read down a column, not across a row: the covariate count matters far less than whether the covariates predict anything.'

rows = []
for k_ in (5, 20, 50):
    a_ = stats.chi2.ppf(1e-4, k_)
    v_ = stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_ + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_)
    row = {"covariates balanced": k_}
    for R2 in (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8):
        row[f"R² = {R2}"] = f"{100 * (1 - np.sqrt(1 - (1 - v_) * R2)):.0f}% smaller"
    rows.append(row)
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("covariates balanced")
```

Translate that into the currency you actually budget in. A standard error 22%
smaller is the precision you would otherwise have bought with **about 65% more
data** — for free, before the study starts. At $R^2 = 0.8$ the same table says
54% smaller, which is worth nearly five times the sample size.

And if $R^2$ is near zero, rerandomization buys you nothing at all. A tidier
baseline table, and nothing else.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What to do

Balance the handful of covariates you genuinely believe predict the outcome —
prior outcome measurements first, since they usually dominate — and keep the
best of **10,000 draws**. Equivalently, threshold at an acceptance rate of 1 in
10,000, which is the $\chi^2_k$ quantile at $p_a = 10^{-4}$.

Do not throw in covariates because you have them. Every one you add has to be
balanced simultaneously, so the acceptance region shrinks in every direction at
once and the balance on the ones you care about gets diluted.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The catch

That gain is not automatic. Rerandomization narrows the true sampling
distribution of your estimate, but a conventional $t$-test does not know that
and will report the wider interval anyway. **Run the standard analysis on
rerandomized data and you give the entire gain back.** Collecting it is what the
second half of this article is about.
:::

## A budget is simpler than a threshold

Picking an acceptance rate means committing to an unbounded loop: you will
*probably* accept within a few thousand draws, but nothing guarantees it.
Fixing a budget — draw 10,000, keep the best — runs in known time and needs no
threshold at all.

Morgan and Rubin recommend exactly this, in §5.2 of their 2015 tiers paper:

> In practice we expect to see little difference between rerandomizing until an
> allocation with $M \le a$ is obtained, and choosing the allocation with the
> smallest $M$ from $1/p_a$ randomizations, where $p_a = P(M \le a)$.

That is offered as an expectation rather than a result — no proof or simulation
is given — so it is worth checking, because the two schemes are genuinely
different. The winner of a tournament of $B$ draws is not guaranteed to clear
the 1-in-$B$ bar, and misses it about $(1 - 1/B)^B \approx 37\%$ of the time.
Best-of-$B$ is always the weaker of the two.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-budget
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: 'Imbalance left behind by the two schemes, as a fraction of what plain randomisation leaves. Lower is better. Best-of-10,000 is never better than thresholding at 1 in 10,000, but the gap closes as covariates are added.'

rows = []
for k_ in (2, 10, 20, 50):
    a_ = stats.chi2.ppf(1e-4, k_)
    v_thresh = stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_ + 2) / stats.chi2.cdf(a_, k_)
    draws = stats.chi2.rvs(k_, size=(3000, 10_000), random_state=rng)
    v_best = draws.min(axis=1).mean() / k_
    rows.append({"covariates k": k_,
                 "threshold at 1 in 10,000": f"{v_thresh:.5f}",
                 "best of 10,000": f"{v_best:.5f}",
                 "ratio": f"{v_best / v_thresh:.2f}x"})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("covariates k")
```

The ratio looks alarming at $k = 2$ — twice the imbalance — until you read the
absolute numbers beside it: $0.00005$ against $0.00010$. Both schemes have
annihilated the imbalance, and doubling almost nothing leaves almost nothing.
The gap only *could* matter at large $k$, where a real fraction of the imbalance
survives, and that is exactly where the two schemes converge: 6% apart at twenty
covariates, 3% at fifty.

So Morgan and Rubin's expectation holds, for a reason their sentence does not
give: the discrepancy is largest precisely where both schemes are already far
better than they need to be. **Pick a budget you can afford and keep the best
draw.**

## What you are actually selecting

With two covariates you can see it. Each dot is one candidate split, placed at
its pair of covariate mean differences. The cloud tilts because height and
weight are correlated — a split over-representing tall people over-represents
heavy ones too — and the acceptance region tilts with it.

At a 5% acceptance rate that region is already a smudge at the origin, which is
the honest visual point. Drag to zoom in on it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-acceptance-zoom
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: 'Each dot is one of 8,000 candidate splits, positioned at its pair of covariate mean differences. The solid ellipse is the 5% acceptance region; the dashed ellipses are the 50%, 20% and 1% regions. Drag the slider to magnify towards the origin.'

N = 200
n_T = N // 2
B = 8000

Xrr = rng.multivariate_normal(mu_hw, S_hw, N)
S_rr = np.cov(Xrr, rowvar=False, ddof=1)
cov_d = (4 / N) * S_rr

idx = np.argsort(rng.random((B, N)), axis=1)[:, :n_T]
s_mat = -np.ones((B, N))
np.put_along_axis(s_mat, idx, 1.0, axis=1)
d_all = (2 / N) * (s_mat @ Xrr)

p_a_main = 0.05
payload = {
    "pts":  np.round(d_all, 4).tolist(),
    "Cinv": np.linalg.inv(cov_d).tolist(),
    "L":    np.linalg.cholesky(cov_d).tolist(),
    "sd":   np.sqrt(np.diag(cov_d)).tolist(),
    "aMain": float(stats.chi2.ppf(p_a_main, 2)),
    "rings": [{"a": float(stats.chi2.ppf(q, 2)), "main": q == p_a_main}
              for q in (0.50, 0.20, 0.05, 0.01)],
    "xlab": "imbalance in mean height (cm)",
    "ylab": "imbalance in mean weight (kg)",
    "colors": {"grey": C["grey"], "green": C["green"], "dark": C["dark"],
               "grid": "#ccd4db", "axis": "#9aa4ad", "tick": "#3f4850"},
}

js = pathlib.Path("acceptance-zoom.js").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
js = js.replace("__ID__", "rz-accept").replace("__DATA__", json.dumps(payload))

display(HTML("""
<style>
.rerand-zoom { margin: 1.2rem 0 1.6rem; text-align:left; }
.rerand-zoom canvas { display:block; width:100%; touch-action:manipulation; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-readout { font-size:.82rem; color:#5b6570; text-align:center;
  margin:.35rem 0 .7rem; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-readout b { color:#21252b; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-sep { margin:0 .6rem; opacity:.45; }
.rerand-zoom input[type=range] { width:100%; margin:0; accent-color:#2c6e9b; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels { display:flex; justify-content:space-between;
  font-size:.82rem; color:#8a929a; margin-top:.3rem; padding:0 9px;
  text-align:left; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span { cursor:pointer; flex:1; text-align:left; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span:nth-child(2) { text-align:center; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span:nth-child(3) { text-align:right; }
.rerand-zoom .rz-labels span.rz-on { color:#2c4a63; font-weight:600; }
</style>
<div class="rerand-zoom" id="rz-accept">
  <canvas></canvas>
  <div class="rz-readout"></div>
  <input type="range" min="0" max="1000" step="1" value="0"
         aria-label="Zoom level, from every draw to the acceptance region">
  <div class="rz-labels">
    <span data-at="0">every draw</span>
    <span data-at="500">3&times; zoom</span>
    <span data-at="1000">10&times; &mdash; the 5% region</span>
  </div>
</div>
<script>""" + js + "</script>"))
```

Zoomed in, the green dots are the splits you would keep. They are not the ones
where both imbalances are near zero — they are the ones inside a *tilted*
ellipse, which tolerates a larger height imbalance when weight is imbalanced the
same way, and is strict about the two disagreeing. That tilt is why the
criterion is a Mahalanobis distance rather than a sum of squared z-scores.

## How to account for it afterwards

Rerandomization changes the design, so it changes what "by chance" means. The
sampling distribution of a difference in means is no longer normal: Li, Ding and
Rubin (2018) show it picks up a truncated term, because the design removed
exactly the part of the imbalance the covariates explain. An ordinary $t$-test
prices in imbalance that is no longer there, so it is *conservative* — and its
intervals are too wide by precisely the factor you were hoping to gain.

The fix is almost disappointingly simple.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Adjust for the covariates you balanced on

Regress the outcome on treatment plus the covariates you used in the design.

Li and Ding (2020) show that once the analysis adjusts for the design variables,
asymptotic normality comes back and conventional standard errors are justified
again — the troublesome term *was* the part of the imbalance those covariates
explain, so regressing on them absorbs it. Your usual tooling then reports the
narrower interval you actually earned.
:::

That is what most practitioners already do by instinct, it costs nothing, and it
works for a difference-in-differences or anything else fitted by least squares.

Two cases need more care. If your estimator is unusual enough that you do not
trust the asymptotics, **randomisation inference** always works: redraw
assignments under the same acceptance rule, refit your model each time, and read
the reference distribution off the results. It needs no new theory and no closed
form — only compute. It is also the honest option if you used a best-of-$B$
budget, since the acceptance rule is then not a simple threshold. Deriving the
Li–Ding–Rubin correction for a bespoke estimator, by contrast, is a research
project rather than an analysis step.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Use the covariate values as they stood when you split

The analysis must use the **pre-randomisation** values of the balancing
covariates, not their latest values.

Suppose you ran a development experiment across villages and balanced on village
population. By the end of the study populations have moved, and if the
intervention worked it may well have *caused* some of that movement, through
migration or falling child mortality. Adjusting for end-of-study population
would be conditioning on something the treatment affected. That is
post-treatment bias: it removes part of the very effect you are measuring, and
it can flip the sign of an estimate.

The design argument agrees. The randomisation distribution is defined by the
acceptance rule, and that rule was evaluated against the baseline numbers. Those
values determine which splits could have occurred, so those are the values the
analysis has to condition on. Freeze the covariate table when you draw the
split, and keep it.
:::

## Three things that will catch you out

**Small samples run out of splits.** There are only $\binom{N}{N/2}$ distinct
equal splits. That is astronomically large at $N = 200$, but at $N = 20$ it is
184,756, and a 1-in-a-million acceptance rate is then not slow but impossible.

**Every covariate is treated as equally important.** $M$ has no way to know that
a baseline outcome measurement matters more than the recruitment site. If some
genuinely matter more, use tiered rerandomization (Morgan and Rubin, 2015),
which applies separate thresholds to groups of covariates in priority order.

**Record everything.** The seed, the covariate table, the encoding, the budget
or threshold. $S$ is computed from the data at hand, so changing the covariate
set changes the metric and therefore which split you would have accepted — and
the inference has to match the scheme you actually ran.
